Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and a domain $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^m$; its admissible nonnegative states are $\Omega_+:=\Omega\cap[0,\infty)^m$. For every ordered pair $i,j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ let $p_{ij},d_{ij}:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be production and destruction transfer rates that are nonnegative on $\Omega_+$. A **finite conservative production destruction system** (finite conservative PDS) is the autonomous ODE

$$y_i'=F_i(y):=\sum_{j=1}^m\bigl(p_{ij}(y)-d_{ij}(y)\bigr),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m,$$

with internal-transfer identities

$$p_{ij}(y)=d_{ji}(y),\qquad p_{ii}(y)=d_{ii}(y)=0.$$

The index $j$ is the donor/source of $p_{ij}$ and the index $i$ is its recipient/destination; $d_{ji}$ is the same transfer viewed as destruction from $j$. The total mass is $M(y):=\sum_{i=1}^m y_i$. The ODE is considered at states in $\Omega_+$. The definition describes a closed system: external sources and sinks must be specified separately and are not included in the conservation claims on this page. No existence, positivity, or regularity assertion about solutions is part of this definition.

Let $m\ge1$, let $(p_{ij},d_{ij})$ be the rates of a finite conservative PDS [[def-finite-conservative-production-destruction-system]] with state domain $\Omega$, and take an input state $y^n\in\mathbb R^m$, a step size $h$, and declared denominators $\sigma_i$. If $y^n\notin\Omega_+$, $h\le0$, or any $\sigma_i\le0$, return an inadmissible-input status before evaluating any rate. Otherwise the **modified Patankar Euler step** returns the unique solution $y^{n+1}$ of

$$y_i^{n+1}=y_i^n+h\sum_{j\ne i}\left(p_{ij}(y^n)\frac{y_j^{n+1}}{\sigma_j}-d_{ij}(y^n)\frac{y_i^{n+1}}{\sigma_i}\right),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.$$

Equivalently, form $M\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ by

$$M_{ii}=1+h\sum_{j\ne i}\frac{d_{ij}(y^n)}{\sigma_i},\qquad M_{ij}=-h\frac{p_{ij}(y^n)}{\sigma_j}\quad(i\ne j),$$

and solve $My^{n+1}=y^n$. The rates in the solve are evaluated only at the admissible state $y^n\in\Omega_+$. For every input passing the branch, return the unique exact solution of the stated linear system. The standard first-order choice is $\sigma_i=y_i^n$, which is admissible only when every $y_i^n>0$. A separately defined rate-factor form extends a first-order step to zero donor coordinates under an additional source-factorization hypothesis.

Let $M=(m_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ for a finite $m\ge1$. Suppose $m_{jj}>0$, $m_{ij}\le0$ for $i\ne j$, and

$$m_{jj}>\sum_{i\ne j}|m_{ij}|\qquad(j=1,\ldots,m).$$

Let $d\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, and consider a first-order IVP and solution in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **one-step method** is a family of maps $\Psi_h(t,v)$, defined for admitted times $t$, positive step sizes $h$, and states $v$, whose value is the method's approximation at time $t+h$ from the single input state $v$ at time $t$. It does not use earlier numerical states.

If $y$ is an exact solution on an interval containing $[t,t+h]$, the **local defect** is

$$\delta_h(t;y):=\Psi_h(t,y(t))-y(t+h).$$

Let $K\subseteq D$ be a fixed compact time-state set. The method has **uniform local order $p$ on $K$ along $y$** if there are constants $C\ge0$ and $h_0>0$, independent of the admitted starting time $t$ and step $0<h\le h_0$, such that

$$\|\delta_h(t;y)\|_2\le C h^{p+1}$$

whenever the exact solution graph on $[t,t+h]$ and the associated method time-state inputs, stages, and outputs under consideration lie in $K$. Here $p$ is a positive integer and $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

The method has **one-step Lipschitz stability on $K$** with constant $L\ge0$ if

$$\|\Psi_h(t,u)-\Psi_h(t,v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$

for every admitted step size $h$, admitted time $t$, and input states $u,v$ with $(t,u),(t,v)\in K$. This is a bound on the change in one step; it is separate from absolute or linear stability regions and does not itself assert a global error estimate.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. Suppose every partial derivative $\partial_jf$ exists on a neighbourhood of $a\in U$ and is continuous at $a$. Then $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$, and $Df(a)$ is the linear map with matrix $Jf(a)$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ be a real matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map
$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

When $n\ge1$, the following three displayed quantities are the same number:

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], axiom (N2)) and
the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

**The value is a finite nonnegative real.** For $n\ge 1$ the norms
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are equivalent by
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]], so there is $C>0$ with
$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_p$,
so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le \bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C\lVert x\rVert_p$;
hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

**The induced infinity norm is a separate named case.** When $m,n\ge1$, define

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

As in the rational-$p$ case, positive homogeneity gives

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

The supremum is finite because for every $i<m$ one has
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

**At $n=0$ the convention is explicit.** The only element of $\mathbb{R}^{0}$
is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the
empty matrix, and the unit-ball definition gives $\lVert A\rVert_{p}=0$.
The unit sphere and the set of nonzero vectors are empty, so the two ratio
formulas above are not asserted in this case.

The induced quantity is a norm on the matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$:
for each rational $p\ge1$, and likewise for the separately named
$\infty$-case when $m,n\ge1$, separation, absolute homogeneity and the triangle
inequality follow from the same three axioms of the underlying vector norm
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

Let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$ and let $m,n,q\in\mathbb{N}$, with the
induced $p$-norms of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

1. **Compatibility.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and every
   $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert Ax\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert x\rVert_p.$$
2. **Submultiplicativity.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and
   $B\in M_{n\times q}(\mathbb{R})$,
   $$\lVert AB\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert B\rVert_p.$$
3. **Normalisation.** For every $n\ge 1$,
   $$\lVert I_n\rVert_p=1,$$
   where $I_n$ is the identity matrix of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]];

Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and a domain $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^m$; its admissible nonnegative states are $\Omega_+:=\Omega\cap[0,\infty)^m$. For every ordered pair $i,j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ let $p_{ij},d_{ij}:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be production and destruction transfer rates that are nonnegative on $\Omega_+$. A **finite conservative production destruction system** (finite conservative PDS) is the autonomous ODE

$$y_i'=F_i(y):=\sum_{j=1}^m\bigl(p_{ij}(y)-d_{ij}(y)\bigr),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m,$$

with internal-transfer identities

$$p_{ij}(y)=d_{ji}(y),\qquad p_{ii}(y)=d_{ii}(y)=0.$$

The index $j$ is the donor/source of $p_{ij}$ and the index $i$ is its recipient/destination; $d_{ji}$ is the same transfer viewed as destruction from $j$. The total mass is $M(y):=\sum_{i=1}^m y_i$. The ODE is considered at states in $\Omega_+$. The definition describes a closed system: external sources and sinks must be specified separately and are not included in the conservation claims on this page. No existence, positivity, or regularity assertion about solutions is part of this definition.

Let $(p_{ij},d_{ij})$ be the rates of a finite conservative PDS [[def-finite-conservative-production-destruction-system]]. A **source-factored transfer representation** on an open set $U\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ containing a compact set $K\subseteq[0,\infty)^m$ consists of functions $a_{ij}:U\to\mathbb R$, $i\ne j$, such that each $a_{ij}$ is $C^2$ on the open subset $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ in the multivariable sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], is nonnegative on $U\cap[0,\infty)^m$, and, for every $y\in U\cap[0,\infty)^m$,

$$p_{ij}(y)=y_j a_{ij}(y),\qquad d_{ij}(y)=y_i a_{ji}(y),\qquad a_{ii}:=0.$$

Here $a_{ij}$ is the transfer rate from donor $j$ to recipient $i$ per unit of donor quantity. Nonnegativity is required on admissible nonnegative states; the $C^2$ extension to the open neighborhood is used for local analysis and need not be nonnegative at inadmissible states with negative coordinates. The factorization is an additional hypothesis, not a consequence of nonnegative rates and the identity $p_{ij}=d_{ji}$. On strictly positive states the ratio $p_{ij}(y)/y_j$ equals $a_{ij}(y)$; at a zero donor coordinate the factorized coefficient remains defined and avoids the indeterminate expression $0/0$.

Let $K$ be a compact nonnegative state set with a source-factored transfer representation [[def-source-factored-production-destruction-rates]]. Given $y^n\in\mathbb R^m$ and a step size $h$, if $y^n\notin K$ or $h\le0$, return an inadmissible-input status before evaluating any factor. Otherwise form $B(y^n)\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ by

$$B_{ij}(y^n)=a_{ij}(y^n)\ (i\ne j),\qquad B_{jj}(y^n)=-\sum_{i\ne j}a_{ij}(y^n).$$

Return the unique solution $y^{n+1}$ of

$$\bigl(I-hB(y^n)\bigr)y^{n+1}=y^n.$$

Equivalently, component $i$ satisfies

$$y_i^{n+1}=y_i^n+h\sum_{j\ne i}\left(a_{ij}(y^n)y_j^{n+1}-a_{ji}(y^n)y_i^{n+1}\right).$$

This procedure uses no denominator $y_j^n$ and is defined when some donor coordinates vanish. It is the factorized extension of the first-order Patankar Euler formula to the zero-state boundary. In exact arithmetic its linear system is uniquely solvable by [[lem-strict-column-dominance-implies-nonnegative-inverse]].

Let $M=(m_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ for a finite $m\ge1$. Suppose $m_{jj}>0$, $m_{ij}\le0$ for $i\ne j$, and

$$m_{jj}>\sum_{i\ne j}|m_{ij}|\qquad(j=1,\ldots,m).$$

Then $M$ is invertible and every entry of $M^{-1}$ is nonnegative. If $b\in\mathbb R^m$ has nonnegative coordinates, then $M^{-1}b\ge0$; if every coordinate of $b$ is positive, then every coordinate of $M^{-1}b$ is positive.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

Let $d\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, and consider a first-order IVP and solution in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **one-step method** is a family of maps $\Psi_h(t,v)$, defined for admitted times $t$, positive step sizes $h$, and states $v$, whose value is the method's approximation at time $t+h$ from the single input state $v$ at time $t$. It does not use earlier numerical states.

If $y$ is an exact solution on an interval containing $[t,t+h]$, the **local defect** is

$$\delta_h(t;y):=\Psi_h(t,y(t))-y(t+h).$$

Let $K\subseteq D$ be a fixed compact time-state set. The method has **uniform local order $p$ on $K$ along $y$** if there are constants $C\ge0$ and $h_0>0$, independent of the admitted starting time $t$ and step $0<h\le h_0$, such that

$$\|\delta_h(t;y)\|_2\le C h^{p+1}$$

whenever the exact solution graph on $[t,t+h]$ and the associated method time-state inputs, stages, and outputs under consideration lie in $K$. Here $p$ is a positive integer and $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

The method has **one-step Lipschitz stability on $K$** with constant $L\ge0$ if

$$\|\Psi_h(t,u)-\Psi_h(t,v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$

for every admitted step size $h$, admitted time $t$, and input states $u,v$ with $(t,u),(t,v)\in K$. This is a bound on the change in one step; it is separate from absolute or linear stability regions and does not itself assert a global error estimate.

A **finite conservative production destruction system** (finite conservative PDS) is the autonomous ODE

$$y_i'=F_i(y):=\sum_{j=1}^m\bigl(p_{ij}(y)-d_{ij}(y)\bigr),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m,$$

with internal-transfer identities

$$p_{ij}(y)=d_{ji}(y),\qquad p_{ii}(y)=d_{ii}(y)=0.$$

The index $j$ is the donor/source of $p_{ij}$ and the index $i$ is its recipient/destination; $d_{ji}$ is the same transfer viewed as destruction from $j$. The total mass is $M(y):=\sum_{i=1}^m y_i$. The ODE is considered at states in $\Omega_+$. The definition describes a closed system: external sources and sinks must be specified separately and are not included in the conservation claims on this page. No existence, positivity, or regularity assertion about solutions is part of this definition.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

A **one-step method** is a family of maps $\Psi_h(t,v)$, defined for admitted times $t$, positive step sizes $h$, and states $v$, whose value is the method's approximation at time $t+h$ from the single input state $v$ at time $t$. It does not use earlier numerical states.

If $y$ is an exact solution on an interval containing $[t,t+h]$, the **local defect** is

$$\delta_h(t;y):=\Psi_h(t,y(t))-y(t+h).$$

Let $K\subseteq D$ be a fixed compact time-state set. The method has **uniform local order $p$ on $K$ along $y$** if there are constants $C\ge0$ and $h_0>0$, independent of the admitted starting time $t$ and step $0<h\le h_0$, such that

$$\|\delta_h(t;y)\|_2\le C h^{p+1}$$

whenever the exact solution graph on $[t,t+h]$ and the associated method time-state inputs, stages, and outputs under consideration lie in $K$. Here $p$ is a positive integer and $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

The method has **one-step Lipschitz stability on $K$** with constant $L\ge0$ if

$$\|\Psi_h(t,u)-\Psi_h(t,v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$

for every admitted step size $h$, admitted time $t$, and input states $u,v$ with $(t,u),(t,v)\in K$. This is a bound on the change in one step; it is separate from absolute or linear stability regions and does not itself assert a global error estimate.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ be a real matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map
$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

When $n\ge1$, the following three displayed quantities are the same number:

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], axiom (N2)) and
the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

**The value is a finite nonnegative real.** For $n\ge 1$ the norms
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are equivalent by
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]], so there is $C>0$ with
$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_p$,
so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le \bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C\lVert x\rVert_p$;
hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

**The induced infinity norm is a separate named case.** When $m,n\ge1$, define

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

As in the rational-$p$ case, positive homogeneity gives

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

The supremum is finite because for every $i<m$ one has
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the
empty matrix, and the unit-ball definition gives $\lVert A\rVert_{p}=0$.
The unit sphere and the set of nonzero vectors are empty, so the two ratio
formulas above are not asserted in this case.

The induced quantity is a norm on the matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$:

inequality follow from the same three axioms of the underlying vector norm
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

By the continuous-partials theorem [F6], these entries have continuous total derivatives through order two. Direct multiplication gives $A(y)y=F(y)$. The matrix $I-hA(y)$ is invertible for $h>0$ by [F4] and equals $I$ at $h=0$; its determinant and cofactors are $C^2$ finite sums of products, and its determinant is nonzero, so the adjugate formula and the scalar reciprocal calculation make its inverse $C^2$ on the compact set of admitted $(h,y)$. It is uniformly bounded there for small $h$. Since $y>0$, [F4] gives $z=(I-hA(y))^{-1}y>0$. The identity $(I-hA)^{-1}=I+hA+h^2A^2(I-hA)^{-1}$ now gives $z=y+hF(y)+O(h^2)$ uniformly; in particular $z-y=O(h)$, so after decreasing $h_0$ we have $z\in V\subset\Omega$ uniformly for $y\in U$. Thus all stage denominators and the final rate evaluations are valid.

Write $B=B(y,z)$ for the final coefficient matrix in [F3]. Its entries are $C^2$ on the compact region of pairs produced inside $V$ by step 1.1: the rates are $C^2$, the stage map is $C^2$, and each reciprocal $z_j^{-1}$ has the same coordinate derivative formulas as in step 1.1. Its columns sum to zero, and direct multiplication using $p_{ij}=d_{ji}$ gives $B(y,z)z=\tfrac12(F(y)+F(z))$. For small $h$, step 1.1 keeps every $z_j$ bounded away from zero, so $B$ and its first derivatives are uniformly bounded. Also $B(y,y)=A(y)$; the mean-value theorem on the compact tube and $z-y=O(h)$ give $B(y,z)=A(y)+O(h)$. The final matrix $I-hB$ is invertible by [F4] and its inverse is uniformly bounded by the adjugate formula. Expanding its inverse yields $\Psi_h(y)=y+hB(y,z)y+O(h^2)=y+hF(y)+O(h^2)$. Comparing with step 1.1 gives $\Psi_h(y)-z=O(h^2)$.

The stage and final maps are $C^1$ in $y$ near the compact positive tube: their rates are $C^2$, their denominators stay bounded away from zero, and their matrix inverses are $C^2$ by the adjugate formula and the reciprocal calculation in steps 1.1–2.1. For any direction $v$, differentiating $z=y+hA(y)z$ gives $(I-hA)D_yz[v]=v+h(DA(y)[v])z$; boundedness from step 1.1 therefore gives $D_yz[v]=v+O(h)$ uniformly for $\|v\|_2\le1$.

Using $\Psi_h-y=hB\Psi_h$, substitute $z$ and use step 2.1 to obtain $\Psi_h-y=hBz+hB(\Psi_h-z)=\tfrac h2(F(y)+F(z))+O(h^3)$. Taylor expansion of $F$ at $y$, together with $z-y=hF(y)+O(h^2)$ from step 1.1, gives $F(z)=F(y)+hDF(y)F(y)+O(h^2)$. Thus $\Psi_h(y)=y+hF(y)+\tfrac{h^2}{2}DF(y)F(y)+O(h^3)$. By [F5]–[F7], the exact solution has the same expansion: $y''=DF(y)F(y)$ and its third derivative is bounded, so the one-variable Taylor remainder applied coordinatewise is $O(h^3)$. Their difference is the asserted uniform exact-start defect in [F9].

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$p_{ij}(y)=d_{ji}(y),\qquad p_{ii}(y)=d_{ii}(y)=0.$$

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

Let $(p_{ij},d_{ij})$ be the rates of a finite conservative PDS [[def-finite-conservative-production-destruction-system]] with state domain $\Omega$. $$y_i'=F_i(y):=\sum_{j=1}^m\bigl(p_{ij}(y)-d_{ij}(y)\bigr),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m,$$

with internal-transfer identities

$$p_{ij}(y)=d_{ji}(y),\qquad p_{ii}(y)=d_{ii}(y)=0.$$

The index $j$ is the donor/source of $p_{ij}$ and the index $i$ is its recipient/destination; $d_{ji}$ is the same transfer viewed as destruction from $j$. The total mass is $M(y):=\sum_{i=1}^m y_i$. The ODE is considered at states in $\Omega_+$. The definition describes a closed system: external sources and sinks must be specified separately and are not included in the conservation claims on this page. No existence, positivity, or regularity assertion about solutions is part of this definition.

If $y^n\notin\Omega_+$, $h\le0$, or any $\sigma_i\le0$, return an inadmissible-input status before evaluating any rate. Otherwise the **modified Patankar Euler step** returns the unique solution $y^{n+1}$ of

$$y_i^{n+1}=y_i^n+h\sum_{j\ne i}\left(p_{ij}(y^n)\frac{y_j^{n+1}}{\sigma_j}-d_{ij}(y^n)\frac{y_i^{n+1}}{\sigma_i}\right),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.$$

Equivalently, form $M\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ by

$$M_{ii}=1+h\sum_{j\ne i}\frac{d_{ij}(y^n)}{\sigma_i},\qquad M_{ij}=-h\frac{p_{ij}(y^n)}{\sigma_j}\quad(i\ne j),$$

and solve $My^{n+1}=y^n$. The rates in the solve are evaluated only at the admissible state $y^n\in\Omega_+$. For every input passing the branch, return the unique exact solution of the stated linear system. The standard first-order choice is $\sigma_i=y_i^n$, which is admissible only when every $y_i^n>0$. Let $(p_{ij},d_{ij})$ be the rates of a finite conservative PDS [[def-finite-conservative-production-destruction-system]].
